transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, tantra, zen, vajrayana, home lightsaber construction, psychedelics, consciousness hacking, non-duality, and all sorts of other stuff. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Joe Hudson. Joe Hudson is an executive coach whose teachings draw from ancient contemplative traditions, modern neuroscience, and psychology. He is a teacher for leaders at such companies as OpenAI, Alphabet, Apple, and more. He is also the founder of Art of Accomplishment, which facilitates experiential courses designed to cultivate ease, joy, and fulfillment in life. And now, without further ado, I give you a conversation with Joe Hudson.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Joe, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Good to be here, Michael.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, good to have you here. We initially talked about doing an episode something like, I don't know, six years ago, and finally the time has come.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: We figured it out.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: We figured it out. So that's great. I'm super happy to have you here. Something that reignited the fire for me is I watch your posts on Twitter. I'm still on X or whatever it's called now. And despite all its problems, I just have kind of been shaping my feed for so long that I just like the stuff I'm reading, and a bunch of the stuff is yours. And more and more I'm like, I like what he's saying there. Oh yeah, that's interesting. And so finally I'm like, I just got to get back on the phone with the guy. So yeah, the stuff that you're putting out is, I think, super interesting and also kind of adjacent. So I'm always talking about meditation stuff and you're more doing coaching. We might say emotional stuff, if you think that's a fair characterization.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: I mean, yeah, my personal journey was there was like 10 years of pretty constant meditation. At least seven of them were basically that's all I did. Make a little money from time to time and sit in a room and meditate. So the stuff I do wouldn't be here without those years of sitting.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, you're talking to a bunch of practitioners. So I'm curious, what sort of sitting were you doing?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: So the first time I ever meditated was a 10-day silent Vipassana, Goenka retreat. And I can tell you a lot about that experience for me. But one of the things that happened was on day five or six, I fell out of the program, right? When you're in your first year of Vipassana, the whole thing is to move the attention from the top of your head to the bottom of your body and back and forth. You're doing a body scan, body scanning, right? And what was happening for me naturally was that my attention was moving through my body and I was following the attention. And it would go all around my body, but it wasn't in this kind of very rigid pattern.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Naughty boy. Yeah. You're not supposed to do that.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Exactly. I went to the teacher and they said, you're not supposed to do that. I was very rebellious. I just, after that, said, I love this meditation, but I'm going to follow what's happening for me. And so from that point on, I just basically let my meditation evolve in its own way. Then I ran across Adya. I had this idea of doing a film that was going to be — this is back before there was like podcasts and YouTube and stuff — I wanted to do a film called Four Fingers, One Moon, because I had been listening to a lot of non-dual teachers from very different traditions and they all had very different ways of pointing to the same thing. And so somehow I met Adya that way and I liked him. He was the first person that I was able to let my guard down with enough to allow myself to be taught. And his meditation practice is like, just don't manage anything, basically a derivative of the Zen, which was his training. And so that just allowed for it to keep on going. So my meditation practice just did — like I followed it more than I was trying to control it, which was a big blessing. And then later on in life, I ran across Dan Brown's work and he has this great article, basically, you know, the integral theory of development, that is a version of that spiral dynamics, or a version of that is Terri O'Fallon's stages. And he basically wrote down, this is the natural stages of meditation. And by this time I'm like, I don't know, 15 years deep or something. And I read it and I was like, yep, yep, yep, yep. And it just like went right up through my experience. It was like, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, until it got to some point where I'm like, I have no idea what the heck he's talking about. And I was like, apparently I'm there on the meditation thing. So I wasn't too much of a follower of one thing. What I did do often, however, is I would find new forms of meditation and try them out for like a week or two. So there's a pretty less known one out of Burma that touched me deeply, which is just noting where your attention is moving. And I did that for a couple of weeks. So I would experiment, I would bring new practices in that I learned from different people or different books. And then I would try them out for a couple of weeks. And then I would go back to following the natural inclination when I sat silent.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Beautiful. And are you still practicing?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah, it's a little bit different now. I'm sure you've had — I would assume you have — multiple people on here who's like, now meditation is something that happens all the time. And that's definitely my experience. And there's still moments where I sit, but my preferred thing is to go off for three or four days and sit silently. I prefer a little bit less on the daily meditation, though it still occurs. I'll still sit for an hour here and there, not at six o'clock in the morning. I'm waking up and meditating like I used to, but now I have a deep desire on a regular basis to go off into the woods by myself and meditate for three or four or five days. And so that's mostly how it expresses through me now.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Wonderful. That sounds super nice.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: So good. So enjoyable.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So I'm curious then, how did you get from doing that — and maybe it overlapped quite a bit, I don't know — but to coaching? If I were to kind of summarize what I see your programs being about, it's more like emotional processing or however you want to describe it. How did that grow out of the meditation, if it did?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah, that's a great question. So I wouldn't describe it that way, though there's a lot of emotions in it. So I was lucky enough to have a very rocky marriage at the beginning. And so we needed to do therapy to make the marriage work. And then once I had this very big experience of oneness that lasted eight seconds during that first meditation retreat, I also became obsessed and fixated on whatever the heck that is. That's what I'm after. And so I did a lot of different kinds of work. I did the Hoffman Process when people still didn't know what the Hoffman Process was. And I tried all sorts of somatic techniques and breathwork stuff. And I started deeply experimenting with any kind of tool I could get my hands on. I don't know, when I was about 25, and I'm now 55, so about 30 years now, something like that. And I still love trying out new tools and experiments. And so there was some sort of like, we're going hand in hand in this, but I was dedicated to the meditation. That was something that was happening for six, seven hours every day for at least seven or 10 of those years. So I was very, very dedicated to that. And then the idea that I'm sure many, many long-term meditators have, it came to me, which is the "what am I" question. I became obsessed with that. And I had asked myself that 10 times a day and contemplate that being that question a lot. And then when that question dissolved, that wasn't really a search anymore. When the search died, so to speak, what happened for me was the moment that question "what am I" got answered — as it is, it's not a logical answer, but it got answered. And the very next thought that I had was, this never ends, which was, I think, a huge blessing for me. That the moment of, oh, I had this eight seconds of oneness and now I have to search to get it back, was a complete pain in the ass. It was a very inefficient route, but one that I needed. But somehow or another, I was rewarded at the end of that journey to be given this gift of "this never ends." And so I never did the thing that a lot of the people around me started doing when they had those awakenings, which was, they thought they were done. They thought it was finished. Like, yeah, that's a problem, because they were searching for peace and the peace was there. And so, hey, I know where to go get peace and I can get it anytime. And like, a lot of people started defining themselves as awake, the people around me. And that lasted for me for like maybe four months, five months. And then I was hanging out with a friend who passed, he wrote a book called Blessed with a Brain Tumor. His name was Will Pye. And he had a meditation teacher who — I can't remember the name, but quite famous — who was like, still worked with depression. And I started to notice there's this distinction between peace and joy.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: And I was like, oh, I don't need anything else. I'm good. But the nature is to evolve. Like the nature of everything is to keep moving. There is no end. And so I just kept moving. The evolution just kept going. And then I ran across a couple people who were — one was deeply into the relational, and the other one, he was this weird guy. He was mostly a photographer. And then he had like one thing on his website. You know, you have those columns on your website: here's my landscapes, here's my woods pictures, here's my portraits. Oh, and here's my teachings. And anyways, I went and experimented with him for a couple of times and his whole thing was, he worked with a lot of Tibetan monks and he's like, yeah, my job is kind of to invite them back into hell. And what he was saying was like, yeah, you can use this as a bypass to a lot of the emotional, psychological work. And I knew that I had done enough of the work to realize that this was never going to end and the evolution continued. And the mythology of finish lines no longer held any sway. But the thing that surprised me about it was that my kind of thinking was there was like one way, maybe two, to have awakening. One was sitting silent meditation a lot. And the other one is, get really depressed and then your psyche cracks and then you see it if you're lucky enough — kind of more of the Byron Katie, Eckhart Tolle.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Eckhart, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: I'm like, these are the ways. And it turns out that's not true. Like in our work, we have people, lots and lots of people, experience awakening through our work.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You can do it through joy. There's many methods.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Exactly. If you think about the awakening — the way that I see it is there's something that's more head related. For convenience, not that there's really any separation, but for convenience and description, I think about the centers as like head, heart, and gut.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: For me, there's a thing that gets confused for people. I hear you saying this, and I just want to put it in the terms I'm always talking about it and run it by you and see how you feel about it or think about it.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That there's actually two axes, two different axes that we're talking about. One is the axis of awakening.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And the other is the axis of liberation, right? Or freedom. And they're different. And what I see happening a lot is people kind of — I'll use the metaphor of drilling a hole. People find a meditation practice and they work at it, work at it, work at it. And let's say it's a good practice, a serious practice, an awakening-focused practice. And they kind of drill a hole down through their stuff, down through their stuff on the cushion. And then they hit some big insight or some kind of clear seeing of their personality as a structure, et cetera. And then that's an awakening.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: I agree with what you're saying.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so much of the time, then the person will go, well, that's it. There it is. I've awakened. And as long as they reproduce those conditions — here I am on my cushion, here I am in a silent retreat or whatever — I can open up that channel down to the awakening. And then there's, as you're calling it, this peace or this spaciousness there. But the minute that they're out of those conditions, let's say kind of to the side of that hole they've drilled, now they're up and walking around, or now they're talking to a person, or now they're doing this or that — the awakening disappears, right? It's there as a memory, but now they're being triggered in various ways by their material. And this is now the realm of the liberation. It's like, no, you got to open up that awakening to cover getting up and walking around, to cover talking to your spouse, to cover all these many, many, many situations. So that instead of it just being this one thing that you do on the cushion under certain conditions, the view that you have come to rest in, in awakening, is there for you all the time, right? It never ends, as you say. And that liberation or freedom — or let's just say at least going in the direction of liberation or freedom, not that it ever is final — requires then working through all your stuff, right? Or maybe "working through" is the wrong way of talking about it, but encountering and bringing the view to that, right, over and over again. So how does that land for you as sort of a way of talking about this?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: I enjoyed it. It's so hard because this is where language starts to fall apart, right? So there was a moment in time where I could no longer in any circumstance identify as what I used to identify as, right? Like the universal consciousness or whatever you want to call that thing, everything and nothing. There was a time when that thing hit that I was like, okay, how do I get that back? It's here, it's not here. Where is it going? I go and ask Adya, like, how do I keep it? All that stuff, right? Then there was a time where it's just always there. So as long as that's a step in the path of liberation, then I can see what you're talking about in your description. I can see, oh, I see how that is an accurate description. If the path of liberation is to get you to that point, then I would see it slightly differently.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. Please say more about that.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. So that moment is the moment where I had this recognition of identifying forevermore, apparently — and we'll see what happens, but it seems like it's forevermore — identifying as the non-personal.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But what I'm getting at is even though that's there all the time, the liberation is whether you're fully involved in a reactive pattern or not, even while that's there.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. So if that's the thought process, then I'm in agreement. And now it's interesting, because then you opened up something else that I want to parse, which is a reactive pattern. I don't think any human being is not constantly in a reactive pattern, meaning we smell coffee, we desire coffee, right? So there's a definition of what is a reactive pattern. And yes, there's this kind of endless thing of becoming more yourself and more authentic and more liberated. I'm not sure if I would define it as non-reactive, but I might — just depends on what you're pointing out. Again, the human language gets a little weird here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. And I'm more interested in how you want to talk about it and how you would unpack it. But I'm not suggesting — if you want to define reactivity in that way, of course we have our learning and our memories and stuff comes up, and we smell coffee or food and our mouth waters and stuff like that. That's always going to go on. I think the thing that was really important in the way I was describing it is whether you're fully caught in that or not, rather than just the fact of it happening. There's a great way of looking at it, which is that that catch gets ever more subtle. It seems like it's asymptotic. The catch becomes more and more asymptotic and less grabby, but yeah.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: The way I think about it — I think that that's a great description as far as how that path goes. And then the thing that I would say is that there's lots of ways to get to the place of seeing through your own identity, and seeing through your own identity permanently, that it's not a coming and going. And emotions can be one of the ways to do that. Relationships can be one of the ways to do that. Joy can be, devotion can be. There's lots of ways because all of them are basically just seeing through the sense of self. Silence is one of the ways to do it, and it's a great way to do it. Meditation is one of the ways to do it. It's a great way to do it, but it's not the only way to do it. And so my work started to become, what are the other ways that we can explore to do that? That one is easier for people to do, because long moments of silence and days off, at least at the beginning, can be incredibly challenging for folks, and we're relational by nature. So how do we do this in a more relational way? And then also, how do we do it in a balanced way where not only are you having the awakening experience, but you also have done some major work on your depression or your procrastination or whatever the issues are, the family-of-origin patterns and society has created in you. And so that became the thing that I became passionate about. That's where I wanted to really do the work. And that's how I got here. And emotions are what I'm most known for. It's definitely not the only thing we do, but I think we're most known for them because they are the most constrained part of the system. Meaning, our society is pretty good at the head, but the emotional part, there's a lot of very low-hanging fruit there. You can get a lot of peace and joy quickly if you learn some basics about the emotions. And so I think that's what makes us known for it, is that that's where a lot of people have gotten a lot of the juice with the least amount of squeeze.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. And that's where I interrupted you. You were starting to talk about — you mentioned sort of three centers, the head, the heart, and the gut, which is a traditional framing, at least those three centers. And I really, really resonate with that, but I interrupted you before you actually unpacked it. So tell me a little bit about that.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: So for me, the awakening that happens primarily in the head is the identification of self, that identification changing — and they can happen separately, together — but it's also not believing your own thoughts anymore. Right? So there's lots of people I know who have this identity that is more universal and they're walking around with it, but they still can't see that every thought that they've ever had is in some way a lie and in some way a truth. And every thought that somebody else has, especially somebody who annoys you, has truth in it and falseness in it. But that's basically the way I see it expressed in the mind, and the development of that. In the heart, it's a development of becoming welcoming of all your emotional experiences. And that leads to a lot of joy. I remember sitting down and talking to Adya, who had become a friend and a huge influence on my life — Adyashanti, for those of you who don't know — and he's like, what are you up to? And I said, oh, we're basically teaching people to fall in love with all their emotional states. And he goes, ah, 90% of the questions I get are that question. I was like, I've been to your retreats, what are you talking about? And he said, 90% of the questions are, how do I feel more of this or less of that? And it hit me, because I went through all the questions in the meditation retreats and that's really what a lot of them boil down to. It's like, how do I feel more of this? And that was a question I was asking, right? How do I feel more of this oneness and less of this constriction? And it's like, oh, right. And so that's what we do on the emotional side: oh, how do you fall in love with, look forward to, can't wait to have every emotional experience.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Let's talk about that a little bit, because what I love about what you're saying is that usually this is framed as "accept all your emotional experiences." There's always this kind of grudging distance and, oh, I don't really want it. And here it's, no, not just accept, not just be okay with, not just sit with, but love. Right? So tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: That's true. Yeah. So let's say I have a child and I want that kid to feel connected and well-behaved, and he comes into the room and I'm like, hey, I accept you. You're okay. How's that shit going to work? Which is basically spiritual for, if I accept you, will you leave?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Totally.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: That's what it is. And so as compared to a child who feels like they are deeply loved and welcomed and they're wanted — that child behaves differently.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I love in the Dan Brown work, he would call that "you take delight in the child."

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. That's great. That gave me some chills. That's a great way to say it. It's a series of sensations. This is both easier and harder to do post the identity shift to universal. It's harder to do because it's easier to repress them or pretend they're not there and go to peace. That's what makes it harder to do. It's easier to do because they're non-personal. So once you get the hang of it, it's this amazing thing. And what you start to realize is it's the resistance to these emotions that causes all the kerfuffle. The pain is in the resistance. The acting out is in the resistance. The behaviors that you're ashamed of is all in the resistance. It's not in the actual emotion. And the emotion is just a set of sensations. So what's the dilemma? And then once you start to accept them and welcome them, then you start noticing, oh, there is huge wisdom in them, and there's data and they have signals and there's an intelligence that they have, which is profound. And they are just like the thoughts in that they are both true and not true. They're pointing to a truth, but they're not wholly true. Thoughts often have the protection of identity in them as a way of being not true, but the emotions have the trauma of our past, which often makes them not true. But if you welcome them and you don't take them as true or personal, but you welcome them — you're like, oh, I can't wait to have this experience — they change in the sensations in the body. They provide a tremendous amount of information. And once you do it with two or three emotions, you start to realize, oh, this is amazing. The other thing that happens, which I think is a more subtle thing and that people have a hard time getting until they get it, is something I call the golden algorithm, which is: the emotion that we're avoiding, we are attracting in the exact way that we're avoiding it. So, example: I'm in my late twenties or mid-twenties, and I was emotionally abandoned as a kid, alcoholic father and mom. So anytime I sniffed that feeling of emotional abandonment, I didn't want to feel it. So I would try to avoid it. And how did I try to avoid it? I'd either get hard, right? Cross my arms. Fuck you, then. Which of course led to more emotional abandonment. Or I'd get needy. Oh, what can I do to please you? Which would lead to more emotional abandonment.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Because people run from the neediness.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Because people run from the neediness. Correct. Yeah. And so this is the case in every one of the emotions that are trying to be avoided. Like, I want to avoid the feeling of being a failure means that I don't take the risks that allow me to be a success. And so I feel like a failure. I don't feel like a failure because I failed at the task. I feel like a failure because I failed at life. But I get to feel like a failure. And so what happens is once you start inviting these emotions and welcoming them and loving them — and love is really the most efficient — what you start realizing is these patterns that you've been living in drop away. Because all of a sudden you're getting emotionally abandoned, you're like, oh, I love feeling emotionally abandoned. Which sounds weird to people, but this is great. This is an experience I really understand. And I can love that just like I can love a child having a bad day. Let's go. And then all of a sudden I don't get hard and I don't get needy. I just stay present with the person and myself. And then the pattern stops or becomes less. And it doesn't really matter if it completely stops, because you're not trying to get rid of it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Joe, this is of course music, music to my ears. And I really, really appreciate the way you're unpacking this. But can we slow down for just a minute and maybe describe for listeners what might sound like a magic X factor? Because I mean, the golden algorithm makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But how do we switch from avoidance and armoring up and trying to get away from, to this seemingly very different place of, oh, I love when this emotion shows up? How do you personally show people how to do that?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. We have a tool for this that I'm happy to give free access to yours. It's called emotional inquiry. But generally what it is, is bringing wonder to the somatic sensations of the emotion. That's it. There's a series that is more effective, like a set of steps that is more effective than other sets of steps. So we codified those. But it's really saying, oh, I am having this experience — instead of going, I know that I don't want it, or I should really want this, or I should love it. It's bringing wonder into this situation. It's just saying, well, what is this thing exactly? So if I say to people, what is fear somatically in your body, what are the sensations of fear? Most people can't really pinpoint it. They can say, oh, fear is electric, or it's in my tummy. They might be able to do that, but they can't say, it's like less dense than anger and more —

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. You don't get a good phenomenological description.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Like, where does it begin? Where does it end? How thick is it? How dense is it? How does it move? What is that sensation of fear really, really like? How do you know where you end and it begins? Think about a kid who finds a frog and they pick it up and they're like, what is this? They sniff it, maybe they even lick it. And they're like, what is this thing? It's like, can you do that with your emotions? And that is often the bridge between "this is something I don't want" to "this is something that I can love" — is just to actually try to figure out what the heck is going on in your system. Really, really understand it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's so cool. So bringing the curiosity, the openness, the wonder.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: And I do use "wonder" here instead of "curiosity." And the semantics that I'm trying to play with here are: curiosity means you're looking for an answer, which is less love. And wonder is, I'm in awe. There is nothing to answer. I'm just like, what is this thing? Let me go and explore this thing.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Because even looking for an answer is this subtle form of wanting it to change.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Or get a handle on it so you can change it. Yeah, exactly.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Exactly. So you have worked with many, many, many people. How long does it take? I think it takes a lot of time for an average person out there to, let's say, work with one of the main emotions they're avoiding to the place where they can actually start to love when it shows up, at least a little bit.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. On average — we have a course called the Great Decisions course, and that's all about that emotional experience. And the reason it is, is because if you read modern neurology, you'll find out that our emotional center of our brain is a default decision-making center in your brain. And that's the case — like, if you burn your hand, you move it without going through that center of your brain. But if you're deciding anything, like where to have lunch or what color pen to use, you're using the emotional center of your brain to do it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. That's how the imaginary scenario gets assessed.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Right. And we're trying to figure out, will this thing make me feel a certain way?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: How many decisions have we made so we feel happier, we don't feel like a failure, or we don't feel rejected? And so we'll do a lot of this work. And that's four or five weeks. And generally it changes most everybody's experience with all of their emotions — if they do the work. So it's not that hard of a thing. There is another piece to it though. And you see this change lives very quickly, which is why I say it's the low-hanging fruit, because it's just not the thing that we're taught and nobody's really teaching it. Yeah. But I have this saying that it's like: before awakening, daddy issues; after awakening, daddy issues. And so what I noticed happens with people is they'll unpack the pattern — like the abandonment pattern that I had, or the failure pattern that I talked about — by learning to love that failure. And then there's a huge amount of freedom. And then whatever it is, six months, a year later, they'll find a more subtle form of that pattern that they get to play with. Right? Now it's not like I'm getting hard from the rejection or I'm getting needy because of the rejection, but now it's, oh, when that person acts the way that my father acted right before I was going to get abandoned, I notice I try to please them, or I notice that I try to — right. And so I'm unpacking a more subtle version of it. So I see the evolution like a corkscrew, right? It's like the stock market and the fact that it goes up into the right and that it's not a straight line. It goes up and down and up and down. So you have to look at the long view to see the progress. But it's also like a corkscrew in the fact that at the top of the corkscrew it's the daddy issue, and at the bottom of the corkscrew it's the mother issue. You're just constantly refining some of these reactions or conditioning that we were raised with.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's so interesting. I'm curious, how would you work with, or guide someone to work with, all their sort of core, woundy, negative self-talk, toxic shame stuff, which comes up so powerfully with this kind of work?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: So on the negative self-talk, we have this program that we're sold out years in advance for, this thing we call Groundbreakers. And it's done in a pretty small group and there's not a lot of people who can facilitate it. So we can't offer it as much as we would like. But in it, we have seven different tools for working with negative self-talk, and we've measured it — a mutual friend of ours actually measured it for us. And we're reducing negative self-talk by a standard deviation, measured three months after the retreat is finished. So we know it's effective, and that's five years of collecting data.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's amazing.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: And interestingly, as we talked earlier, there's lots of ways of seeing through the identity. One of them is to see through the voice in your head, the repetitive negative voice in your head. And so in that, it's not uncommon for like one in 12, maybe one in 16 people to have a deep awakening experience in one of those retreats. And so I'll talk to you about some of the tools we've used. I try to be a little careful about sharing these tools. We have probably, I think, 12 at this point, but a lot of them are really container-specific, meaning they really work well if there is a whole bunch of unconditional love around you, and they don't work so well if you're all by yourself doing them in a room. The context means a lot with emotional work. So for instance, there's all those studies that show if I start moving my anger, I'm angry more often — which is totally true in the short term. It's not true in the long term, is my experience. We haven't done a study on it, but my experience is that in the long term, movement of anger reduces the amount of anger that you're feeling towards yourself and towards others. Anger towards self is negative self-talk. Anger done in a way that recreates the shame totally creates more anger. Anger done in a way that doesn't create shame, that doesn't break anything, that doesn't hurt anybody, that doesn't scare anybody, that isn't manipulating anybody — that's just the movement of the energy with love — that reduces the amount of anger that we have on a regular basis. So the context is incredibly important for all this work. But I have a couple that I can share around the negative self-talk. What I noticed is that most people try to change the negative self-talk, and I find that incredibly ineffective. But if you change the way you react to the self-talk, that's incredibly effective. And the best way to do it is to experiment and learn how different ways of reacting to it create different responses from the voice. So most people listen to their negative self-talk the way that you would listen to a politician. So just imagine the politician that you hate most on the planet. Imagine the person who you think is brainwashed by them listening to that politician going, yep, uh-huh, okay, mm-hmm, yep, yep, yep, that's what we got to do. That's how most people listen to their negative self-talk. They don't question it. They agree with it. Maybe they rebel against it and don't do what it says. "You should work out more." Okay, I should work out more. I'm not going to work out more. That's like the typical reaction that people have to the negative self-talk once they know that it's there. Another way you could react to it is say, wow, you're a horrible manager. You've been doing this for 10 years and it hasn't worked. You haven't even tried anything new. Every time it says something, you could respond that way. Or every time it says something, you could respond with, no. Or every time it says something, you could respond with, I see how scared you are and I'm right here with you. Or every time it says something, you could say, huh, I wonder if that's true. You could have a thousand different reactions to it. So if you can write down 20 of those reactions that you would like to try — one of my favorites is "ouch," just say ouch every time it says something mean — then run each experiment for three days. You'll learn a ton and the voice in your head will be different. That's one of the tools that's very easy to use. It works well if you're working by yourself in it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So harder to mess up on your own.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Correct. Just doesn't require the context to make it effective or safe. Yeah. You can also just ask yourself the question whenever you hear anything it says, like, would I say that to anybody else? And if not, why? What would make me not say it? There's lots of cool tools. But the trick to the negative self-talk is there's three components of it. The first one is, how do you react to it? The second one is identifying it. For me, it was very easy when I had a big experience where the negative self-talk got reduced by like 75%. I was like, wow. And it took me a long time to realize that there was still the other 25% there, right? That the "have you done this yet? Have you done this yet? Oh, you got to also do that" — that was also negative self-talk. I thought that was just like, you know —

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Getting stuff done. Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Just getting shit done. So there's the identification of it. Another example of this is, oh, you can do it. You got this, you know? Yeah, I believe in you. Like, would you say that to Michael Jordan? Would you? No. That assumes that there's something wrong that has to be fixed.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a little condescending.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. So there's a whole bunch of unpacking of what it is. And then there's the, how do I want to react to it? And then the other part of it is the emotional content of it. A lot of the self-talk is to prevent us from feeling an emotion, or is an expression because an emotion isn't being felt. So shame is anger turned inward, which means that if we're in a big shame thing, we're probably not getting angry in a clean way outwardly — meaning not at anybody, not hurting anybody, not controlling anybody. Or anxiety or fear. We might worry and have this "have you done this? Have you done this? Why aren't you doing that?" And that anxiety is just the unfelt fear, and existential fear of our existence. Like, we're not going to be okay. As it turns out, the only thing that's a hundred percent clear in this world is that we're not going to be okay. And so can you feel that emotion? So there's a lot of components to really having a different relationship with the negative self-talk, but those are a couple of tools.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thanks for sharing those, Joe. That's really fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: By the way, for the meditators in the room, I think it was Adya who used to say this. He's like, meditation can be self-management, but we should call that torture. And so for me, meditation was just like letting the self-abuse off the leash. It was just constant, which was great in the fact that I got to see it. I got to be aware of it. I got to know, oh wow, this is happening inside of me. But what I didn't get for a long time is there is an emotional experience underneath that that I am not feeling. And you'll see this when we run these retreats. You'll see these people have these emotional experiences and their minds are quieter than a room full of meditators. It's just like, nobody even wants to talk. You're in a room full of meditators and you say, oh, does anybody have any questions after a meditation, and people are going to talk and there's going to be this relief in the talking. And if you're in a room full of people who've just had a really clean, beautiful, shame-free expression of emotion, you're like, is there any questions? And nobody says anything. Like I've been there with a room of 200 people and they're just like a 10-minute pause. Nobody asks a question. And it's very still.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Very still. Yeah. It's so cool. I have about 600 questions right there. I want to hear kind of your view on certain things.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Let me at least ask you — you're talking about avoiding certain feelings and/or repressing or denying emotions, or resistance to emotion. And the context of that is usually bad emotions. But what about the other direction, where the kind of greediness or grasping or hanging on to good emotion? There's real friction there. You know, I don't want it to go away, or I want to get it. How do you model that and how are you helping people with that?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: I look at that completely differently. So I agree that the outward expression is grasping. What I've noticed is, take somebody who's jealous of their partner. They're sexually jealous. Don't look at him. Don't dress that way. Whatever it is. They're doing something that I would say is you put one hand out in a "stop" and you have another hand saying, come to me, come to me, come to me. That is a form of pushing somebody away, just like my neediness is a way of pushing something away. My experience is that the grasping on the external is "I want it, I want it, I want it, I want it," but subconsciously it's a pushing away. And so it's really easy to intellectually accept that I want to feel happy, and it's very hard to intellectually accept, I want to feel angry. Like, I look forward to, I love, I welcome anger — hard to intellectually accept. Easy to intellectually accept: I want to feel joy. Physically, anger is a far easier thing to accept than joy. So I have this very specific way in which we do anger release in our live programs and in some of our virtual programs. And you will see people go for 40 minutes of releasing anger. And then we're like, okay, now we're going to do pleasure. And everybody is spacing out inside of like five minutes. And so the obliteration of identity is far greater in feeling, accepting, and welcoming the intensity of a positive emotional experience than it is a negative one.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Oh, I think that's totally true. Like we lose ourselves. Like you have a certain sense of bliss occur and there's a part of you that can't get recovered. It's totally true. It's why real devotion work is such a powerful awakening direction.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Exactly. So mentally people are like, of course I want to feel joy. And of course, how on earth could you want to feel abandoned? But physically the abandonment is far easier to feel. And so what you'll notice is that typically when people are starting to open up their emotional — what I call emotional fluidity — and going through the stages of development of the emotions (and I have a podcast if you want to geek out on that), is that they go from, depending on the society, but usually the first is anger or sadness, right? So one's easier for men in certain cultures, one's easier for women in certain cultures, and vice versa. And then they move into fear, and then they move into things like peace or bliss or joy or love, deep love. And the identity gets far more crushed in that. And it's the same process. It's, can I be in wonder? Can I fully embrace this intensity? Can I welcome it? Can I savor? Can I be in gratitude for? And you start noticing the grasping is as much resistance — grasping for it to stay, or pushing it away. Both are equal in the resistance game.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. That's so interesting. I mean, that's definitely what I was asking towards, is the fact that that same kind of push-pull is there, even if we often think about it very differently. But people are resisting it or trying to control it or deny it or whatever. So yeah, that's really, really interesting. Another thing I wanted to bring up is the whole idea of what I would call complete experience of an emotion, where instead of something that you're controlling and denying and resisting and having all kinds of judgment and opinions about, you instead are feeling it fully. And it's kind of, let's just say, clean and clear. Sometimes that's talked about as transforming the emotion or something. And I don't really see it as it transforming exactly, but more like you're really actually fully having a complete experience of it, where you start to understand that sense of transformation is the complete experience of it. It's really different. Really different. And I think for me, the thing that's so different about it is, it's like if you burn something and there's no soot left over or no smoke, it's not leaving any residue. In fact, it's kind of the opposite. It's incredibly clean.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Gives you energy.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. And energy in a kind of openness anyway. So I'm curious how you would talk about that.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: My metaphor on this one is, let's use anger as an example. You think of it as a tube, and here's this energy flowing through this tube or hose or something. And you can kink it one way, and it sounds like this: "It's a nice dress." And you can kink it another way, and it's like, "oh well, that's just such an adorable outfit, isn't it? I mean, for the country, that's a great outfit." And you can kink it another way and it's "you motherfucker, you fucking asshole, I will kick your fucking ass." And you can kink it another way and it's "I'm not angry." But if it's unkinked, it feels like Gandhi or Martin Luther King or Mother Teresa. It is boundaried. It is a non-acceptance. It's clarity. It's determination. And so I can see why people say it's transformed, but it's the same energy, just unresisted.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. Yeah. It's not like you've turned it into something else, which would be, in fact, a kind of resistance.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. I had a Tibetan practitioner tell me once that there's like the five sins — they don't call them the sins thing, the five impurities or something, I don't know the words — and then you find out that they're the same thing as the five virtues. And he was just describing, when I told him that story, he said, this is basically how we describe it: the five gems and the five impurities, or something like that. But it's the same thought process. And you see it also in traditional Chinese medicine, this thought process of the emotional experience having this clean form that is really enlivening. My other experience is that the more emotional fluidity I have, the harder it is — like the distinction between the emotions gets a little bit, you know, it's not as clear, because there's a kind of a love in all of them, if you will, or an acceptance, expansiveness in all of them.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So yeah, you're talking about the five Buddha families really. And each of them has a kind of unawakened form of emotion that turns into an awakened form of emotion. For example, anger becomes clarity is a really common one. Or fear becomes a kind of pure energy, a lot of energy. And so that's how that's talked about all the time. Although there's only five of them, and I'm like, well, actually there's a lot more emotions than five.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: That's an interesting one, because I could geek out on that all the time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Please do.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. There's a book called The Neuroscience of Emotions and they do these heat maps of different emotions that are oddly consistent throughout humanity. And then there's the internal experience. And the way I view it is like the color chart, which is, all the colors come from three or five emotions, and everything else is just the combination of those. What I know is that there was a time in my life where labeling the emotions allowed me to feel the emotions more fully. And then there was a time in my development when naming the emotions prevented me from feeling the emotions more fully. And I'm pretty confident on one level I've maybe only ever felt five emotions, and on another level I've never felt the same emotion twice. So this one, from an internal experience, is a very interesting one to try to describe. And from an external, apparently there's heat maps that can have a physiological answer to the question.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It is very fascinating. Way back when, there was a student of Margaret Mead who became quite famous. And post-World War II, the idea that anything was sort of genetically determined in human beings was really, really not acceptable to talk about. And so the idea was that all emotions are socially constructed. And so this student, Paul Ekman, went to New Guinea and found these people in remote villages and showed them movies of, I think it was just Americans or Westerners having certain emotions, and showed them photos of people having emotions. And was really frustrated because they had no trouble naming the emotions at all. I think the only one they got confused with was the eyes wide open for surprise and fear. That was the only one, because obviously that's the look when a lion jumps out of the — and the look of a birthday party, right? A surprise birthday party. And so it was the beginning of the switching of the whole thesis and coming back to something more like what Darwin had outlined in his last book — which interestingly was the first modern bestseller and the first book to have photographs in it — which was The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Well, I've never read that. That's amazing. I've gotta read that book. Wow.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. He's just like, look, emotional expression didn't come from nowhere. And it has this evolutionary background and so on and so forth. Very, very interesting. And of course it's a book from the 1800s, so there's problematic parts of it.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Of course. Of course. The other thing about the Paul story that I really dig — and again, I'm older, but this is how I remember it — was that he had a mentor, Paul, and Paul's mentor would look at tribal people from around the world. And he could look at a picture of them and he could tell you what was happening in their society. I remember hearing that and going, what? And when people watch me coach, they think it's magic, because I have this way of reading people that seems like, how would you possibly ever know that thing? And some of it's pattern recognition, and some of it is stuff I can't explain. But a grand majority of it is that, outside of the facial expression, emotions — chronically repressed emotions, any emotions held back — require musculature.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Like if I say, hey, don't feel any emotion — some people might try to meditate as a way to not feel emotions — you watch your body and there's an emotion, you don't want it, you have to clamp down. And so there's a musculature holding. And if that is chronic, it shapes your body. Oh look, that's the critical parent hunch. Oh look, that's the scared tuck of the butt. Oh look, there's the repressed anger that happens in that one line in the face over the nose. There's the book called The Body Keeps the Score, but our bodies are actually walking symbols of our emotional repression. And it's amazing. So now I understand how this person could look at a picture and say, yeah, there's some pedophilia in that culture, and be accurate. Because you really can read a tremendous amount in somebody's body, because that chronic holding of an emotion changes us.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. It is held there and you can even work on it there. So most of the audience for this podcast is meditators, as we've been talking about. I can't imagine they'd be listening to it if they weren't. And if you are a listener who doesn't meditate at all, please write me and tell me why — especially over many episodes. But I'm curious. I think, of course, the big monster under the bed, the big boogie monster for meditators these days, is bypassing. Oh, you're bypassing.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And my response to this is often, why is that special in meditation? I mean, people are bypassing all the time. Why is it only a problem when you're meditating? My response to it is, oh, don't worry. It'll be there when you get to it. It ain't going anywhere until you address it. Just bypass all you want. It'll be there.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: It's waiting for you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's waiting for you. But I'm curious, I'm sure you run into this quite a bit. And so imagine you're talking to a room of only meditators. How would you talk about this particular thing and what to do about it?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: I would say, what makes you think you're more powerful than gentleness?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so please unpack that a little bit.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. Somehow or another, your will on what to pay attention to, your goals, you telling yourself not to avoid — basically some form of self-criticism saying, don't avoid this thing anymore, this other person don't avoid this thing anymore — that will is more powerful, more effective than gentleness. And so there's a huge amount of hubris in that. There's a lot of identity in that. There's a lot of like, I'm the one who's going to create my own awakening in that. Instead of — right — a kid can learn to walk without that. A kid can learn to talk without that. A bird can migrate across a thousand miles without that. And somehow or another, you can't just allow the gentleness to take care of it. And the reason that I position it that way is, generally the reason that they're avoiding it is because they're not gentle with themselves on that issue, right? That bypassing is usually shame. It's usually something that brings up shame in them, where they're particularly non-gentle with themselves. And so somehow or another, I'm going to shame myself, then beat myself up for not paying attention to the thing that I'm ashamed of, so that I can then feel more shame over not attending to this thing — is somehow a more powerful mechanism of creating awareness than being gentle, allowing gentleness to guide you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And please talk a little bit about allowing gentleness to guide one.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah. This is a challenging one, especially for people in spiritual circles or meditators. You use any words you want to use and someone's going to figure out a way that they need to do it. So it's like surrender. Okay, I got to surrender. How do I surrender? What am I going to do to surrender? Gentle — how do I be gentle? What do I have to do to gentle? What's the checklist for being gentle? The closest that I have is to receive. Like, how do you receive? How do you lay down on your bed and receive? Right now, as you're sitting, listening to this, what do you need to do to just receive? Whether you want to receive — I don't care what you're saying — let's call it receiving the experience of this moment, or receiving the wisdom of your somatic world, or receive the sensations in your body. What is it to just receive? And that's gentleness. That's the opposite of enforcing your will. It's being in the pure receptivity of it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's beautiful, Joe. Thank you for sharing that. Really feeling that. Yeah. So we're going to have to bring this to a close here. Okay. But I'm curious —

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Have to? I don't know, Michael. We don't have to do shit. But I know we're at the end of our time, but we can rebel. I have a three-year-old waiting to talk to me, so I'm not sure how good that's going to go.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Oh, good for you.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah, no, it's exciting. I want to go see him do some lightsaber fighting.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But I'm curious, how do people learn more about you and maybe your programs?

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: Yeah, the best is to go to artofaccomplishment.com. That's a great way to do it. If you want to watch the coaching and see what kind of transformation is possible, the YouTube has tons of coaching and teaching videos. And we have a podcast as well. So since people hear podcasts — and I think we're at a hundred and something episodes and almost all of them are teaching episodes. The way I think about how to work in our ecosystem is, think about the thing that's bothering you the most in your life and find some episode or some coaching or some teaching on that thing, and start there, and then wander around from that place. But if you can pick the thing that's the biggest issue — and we have episodes on awakening and we have episodes on what to do after awakenings and we have episodes on anger and we have episodes on getting in fights with your wife or husband — so we have episodes on a lot of stuff. So find something and then dig in there where there's the most pain, because that's where your consciousness is calling you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Wonderful. Thank you so much again, and hoping to talk to you again soon, Joe.

transcript.speaker: Joe Hudson
transcript.text: What a pleasure. Thanks for having me.
